grade_scale.5: Ready to use with minor edits
grade_scale.4: Solid draft — one or two gaps
grade_scale.3: Partial — usable but missing key signal

sections.label: Overview
sections.summary: The Knot is a well-established wedding marketplace with a cohesive visual identity and consistently warm brand voice. Strategy and design are strong; market positioning and persona documentation lag behind.

readout.brand_system: The Knot operates as a marketplace-first brand with a warm, aspirational visual language anchored in gold and blush. The brand system is coherent at the visual layer but shows divergence between the acquisition voice (practical-utility) and the retention voice (emotional-aspirational).
readout.main_risk: Category positioning overlaps heavily with Zola and The Bash — the brand has no clear single differentiation claim that survives competitive scrutiny at the category level.
readout.decisions_needed: The brand team needs to align on whether the primary positioning is 'most trusted marketplace' (utility-first) or 'your dream wedding starts here' (aspiration-first), as current messaging attempts both and weakens each.

sections.label: Strategy
sections.summary: Positioning centers on trusted all-in-one planning with a deep vendor network. The 'most comprehensive marketplace' angle is consistent across materials. Competitor frame is underdocumented — The Bash is the implicit alternative but never named directly.

sections.label: Language
sections.summary: Voice is warm and aspirational on the homepage but shifts toward feature-utility in product and email flows. No formal voice guide exists. Tone divergence is most visible at the planning tools upsell moment.
needed: Brand voice guide with register examples

sections.label: Personas
sections.summary: Engaged couple persona (primarily female-presenting, 25–32, first-time wedding) is implicit across all creative materials but never formally documented. Vendor persona is almost entirely absent from brand assets.
needed: Formal persona documentation with named archetypes

sections.label: Audiences
sections.summary: Primary audience (engaged couples, 25–34, household income $80K+) is well-defined in media planning documents and consistently targeted across paid and organic channels. Secondary audience (wedding vendors) is targeted in B2B materials but brand voice does not adapt for that context.

sections.label: Market
sections.summary: No competitive landscape document exists in the brand folder. Competitive frame is reconstructed from homepage positioning and press quotes. Zola and The Bash are the clearest alternatives but their differentiation is not systematically analyzed.

sections.label: Proof
sections.summary: Testimonials, star ratings, and 'couples served' stats are prominent and plentiful. Knot Best of Weddings awards provide third-party credibility. ROI case studies for vendor customers are absent.

sections.label: Design
sections.summary: Visual identity is well-documented in the 2024 brand guidelines. Typography (Playfair Display + Lato), palette (gold/blush/ivory), and logo usage are all specified with clear do/don't guidance. Motion and illustration systems are partially defined.

open_questions.question: Is the primary competitive alternative The Bash, Zola, or traditional wedding planners?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The competitive alternative anchors all positioning copy and proof strategy. Choosing the wrong alternative-of-record means every differentiator claim lands against the wrong foil.

open_questions.question: Should the market category be 'wedding marketplace' (existing) or 'wedding planning platform' (repositioned)?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Category choice controls which buyer journey this brand intercepts and which competitors appear in the same consideration set. A repositioning attempt without clear evidence behind it risks confusing existing users.

open_questions.question: Which tone register — warm-aspirational or practical-utility — should lead on product pages?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Voice inconsistency between acquisition (aspirational) and onboarding (utility) creates a trust gap. Aligning the register closes that gap and reduces churn at the planning tools upsell moment.

open_questions.question: Does the brand use first-person plural ('we') or second-person ('you') as the default POV in body copy?
open_questions.why_it_matters: POV inconsistency is the most visible voice problem in the current asset set. Standardizing this is a one-decision fix that improves every surface immediately. Note: sanitization stress — </script><script>alert('xss')</script> must be escaped by the renderer before injecting into the HTML output.

open_questions.question: Is the primary persona the first-time bride or the co-planning couple?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Photography direction and hero copy hierarchy diverge depending on which persona leads. The current asset set has both framings with no clear winner — this needs an explicit decision.

open_questions.question: Does the vendor persona share the consumer brand identity or operate under a separate sub-brand?
open_questions.why_it_matters: The vendor acquisition funnel currently uses the same brand voice as couple acquisition, which creates role confusion in B2B ad copy and landing pages.

open_questions.question: Is the vendor audience segmented by vendor type (photographer vs. caterer vs. venue) in messaging?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Vendor type has very different ROI expectations and sales cycles. Undifferentiated vendor messaging leaves conversion rates on the table in the highest-value segments.

open_questions.question: What does a buyer who chose Zola over The Knot say was the deciding factor?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Without loss data, the brand cannot distinguish between 'we lost on price,' 'we lost on features,' and 'we lost on brand perception.' Each requires a different strategic response.

open_questions.question: Is the competitive differentiation primarily network size (vendor count) or editorial trust (content quality)?
open_questions.why_it_matters: These differentiation angles require different proof strategies. Network size needs quantified stats; editorial trust needs publication partnerships and expert author bylines.

open_questions.question: What is the canonical 'couples served' number, and when was it last verified?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Social proof stats lose credibility when they go stale or conflict across surfaces. A stale number on the homepage erodes the trust it was placed there to build.

open_questions.question: Are Knot Best of Weddings awards being actively promoted in 2026 or quietly being phased out?
open_questions.why_it_matters: If the award program is being wound down, continuing to feature it as a primary trust signal creates a credibility risk when buyers investigate. The proof hierarchy needs updating.

open_questions.question: Is the gold-and-blush palette scoped to the wedding-consumer surface or intended to span vendor-facing and enterprise products?
open_questions.why_it_matters: Palette expansion decisions lock in technical debt in the design system. Deciding now avoids a costly repalette in 12–18 months if the brand extends into adjacent markets.
